subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on Food, Nutrition and Health, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain Food, Nutrition and Health for GCSE Edexcel Food Preparation & Nutrition simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the main function of protein in the body?
options: Growth and repair of body cells and tissues
Helping blood to clot after injury
Insulating the body against heat loss
Providing the body's main source of energy
questions.explain: Protein's primary role is the growth and repair of cells and tissues; it can be used as a secondary energy source only if too much is eaten.

questions.q: Which food is a source of high biological value (HBV) protein?
questions.explain: HBV proteins contain all the essential amino acids; they come mainly from animal sources such as eggs, meat, fish and dairy, plus soya and quinoa. Beans, lentils and bread are LBV.

questions.q: A vegan combines rice with beans in one meal. What is this an example of?
questions.explain: Protein complementation combines two LBV plant proteins whose missing essential amino acids complement each other, giving the overall value of an HBV protein.

questions.q: Which type of fat is usually solid at room temperature and mainly from animal sources?
questions.explain: Saturated fats (e.g. butter, lard, suet) are solid at room temperature and come mainly from animals; a high intake is linked to raised blood cholesterol and CHD.

questions.q: Which food provides mainly unsaturated fat?
questions.explain: Unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature and mostly from plants and oily fish; olive oil is a good source. Butter, lard and suet are saturated.

questions.q: Which of these is a source of complex (starchy) carbohydrate?
questions.explain: Starchy foods like pasta, rice, potatoes and bread are complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly. Sugar, honey and jam are simple (free) sugars.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of dietary fibre (NSP) in the diet?
options: It aids digestion and prevents constipation
It builds strong bones and teeth
It provides a fast source of energy
questions.explain: Fibre adds bulk, helps food move through the digestive system, prevents constipation and reduces the risk of bowel disease. It is found in wholegrains, fruit, vegetables and pulses.

questions.q: Vitamin D is needed for which function?
options: Absorption of calcium for bones and teeth
questions.explain: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, which is essential for strong bones and teeth. It is made in the skin from sunlight and found in oily fish and eggs. A deficiency causes rickets.

questions.q: A person suffers from poor vision in dim light. A deficiency of which vitamin is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Vitamin A is needed for vision in dim light and for healthy skin and immunity. It comes from liver, dairy and orange vegetables (as beta-carotene).

questions.q: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is important because it helps the body to:
questions.explain: Vitamin C aids iron absorption, wound healing and protects cells as an antioxidant. It is found in citrus fruit, blackcurrants and peppers. Severe deficiency causes scurvy.

questions.q: Which preparation mistake is most likely to reduce the vitamin C content of vegetables?
options: Boiling for a long time in lots of water
questions.explain: Vitamin C is water-soluble and destroyed by heat, so long boiling in plenty of water causes large losses. Steaming and quick cooking preserve more of it.

questions.q: Which mineral is essential for making haemoglobin in red blood cells?
questions.explain: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood. Good sources include red meat, liver and dark leafy greens. A deficiency causes anaemia.

questions.q: Eating too much sodium (salt) is most closely linked to which health problem?
questions.explain: A high salt (sodium) intake raises blood pressure, increasing the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease. Adults should have no more than 6g of salt per day.

questions.q: A teenager avoids all dairy products. Which mineral are they most at risk of lacking?
questions.explain: Dairy is a key calcium source, needed for bones and teeth. Avoiding it risks low calcium, so alternatives such as fortified plant milks or leafy greens are needed.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of water in the body?
questions.explain: Water regulates temperature, transports nutrients and removes waste, but it provides no energy (no calories). Dehydration causes headaches, tiredness and dark urine.

questions.q: What does EAR stand for in nutrition?
questions.explain: EAR (Estimated Average Requirement) is the average daily energy or nutrient requirement estimated for a group of people of a given age and sex.

questions.q: If energy taken in from food is regularly greater than energy used, what is the likely result?
questions.explain: When energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, the surplus is stored as fat and body weight increases, which over time can lead to obesity.

questions.q: A diet high in saturated fat and salt increases the risk of which condition?
questions.explain: High saturated fat raises blood cholesterol and high salt raises blood pressure, both increasing the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).

questions.q: Which change would best reduce a person's risk of developing type 2 diabetes?
options: Eating more free sugars and staying inactive
Maintaining a healthy weight and cutting sugary foods
questions.explain: Type 2 diabetes risk is reduced by maintaining a healthy weight, being active and lowering free-sugar intake; obesity and high sugar intake are major risk factors.

questions.q: Why do teenagers have a particularly high need for calcium and iron?
options: They are less active than adults
Rapid growth and, for girls, menstruation increase demand
questions.explain: Adolescents grow rapidly and lay down bone mass, raising calcium needs; menstruation in girls increases iron needs to replace blood loss and prevent anaemia.
